extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, literary critics, students of theatre and readers interested in the principles of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance for producing and evaluating comic drama and literature: principles about audience, comic temperament, characterization, style, moral purpose, and stage practice drawn from historical examples (Molière, Congreve, Shakespeare, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivated-audience requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A society of cultivated men and women is required, wherein ideas are current and the perceptions quick, that he may be supplied with matter and an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy needs an audience with intellectual activity and quick perceptions; 'merely giddy communities, and feverish emotional periods, repel him.' Score comedies partly by how well they assume and address a discerning public; anti-patterns are works aimed at a wholly undemanding or merely noisy crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natal gift of subtlety in the comic poet
rubrics_metrics.description: To touch and kindle the mind through laughter, demands more than sprightliness, a most subtle delicacy. That must be a natal gift in the Comic poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good comedy aims at the head (intellect/subtlety) rather than only the sides (bodily laughter). Evaluate whether the comic voice penetrates subtly rather than relying on loud, obvious gags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual acuteness of poet and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: He must be subtle to penetrate. A corresponding acuteness must exist to welcome him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great comedy depends on both skill in the writer and receptivity in the audience; measure success by whether the work rewards an attentive, reflective audience rather than only immediate laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of making 'respectable' people laugh
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘C’est une étrange entreprise que celle de faire rire les honnêtes gens,’ Molière says; and the difficulty of the undertaking cannot be over-estimated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy that convinces cultivated, decorous audiences is especially praiseworthy; works that only appeal to base or sensational impulses are less valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering to extremes (agelasts and hypergelasts)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are men ... agelasts (non-laughers) ... and hypergelasts (excessive laughers) ... to laugh at everything is to have no appreciation of the Comic of Comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write to please only those who never laugh or those who laugh at everything; successful comedy discriminates and cultivates taste, rather than pandering to extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle-distance perspective (balance between opponents)
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall find ourselves about where the Comic spirit would place us, if we stand at middle distance between the inveterate opponents and the drum-and-fife supporters of Comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A balanced, measured stance between moralistic denunciation and raucous celebration yields a better environment for comic genius; evaluate tone for this equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe manners and generalize (Horatian/Molière principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe the manners of his age and give his characters the colour befitting them at the time ... by slightly raising and softening the object of study ... generalized upon it so as to make it permanently human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good comedy studies contemporary social manners, then elevates and generalizes them (not slavish realism) so characters become permanently human types; anti-pattern: raw, unfiltered portraiture that lacks generalizing insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid raw realism / vulgar realism
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unwholesome for men and women to see themselves as they are, if they are no better than they should be: and they will not, when they have improved in manners, care much to see themselves as they once were. That comes of realism in the Comic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive realism that merely exposes worst features without moral or imaginative shaping is a flaw; prefer comedies that transform or interpret reality rather than merely mimic its vulgarities (examples: critique of Wycherley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy must have an idea (life of the comedy is in the idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fable is thin. The life of the comedy is in the idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess comedies by the central idea that animates them; a thin plot without an informing comic idea is weak. Example: Misanthrope’s life is its idea rather than plot contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral should be embedded, not preachy
rubrics_metrics.description: His moral does not hang like a tail, or preach from one character incessantly cocking an eye at the audience, ... but is in the heart of his work, throbbing with every pulsation of an organic structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good comic works integrate moral critique into character and structure rather than add moralizing tags or stage-asides; penalize works where morality is tacked-on or overtly didactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth over surface wit: genuine humour vs. mere cleverness
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Genuine humour and true wit require a sound and capacious mind, which is always a grave one.' Contrast: Congreve's surface wit vs. Molière's deeper spring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish wit that springs from understanding and humane insight (valued) from merely prepared one-liners or intellectual fireworks (less valuable). Example of anti-pattern: mechanical epigrams that feel schoolboyish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit should vindicate reason, common-sense, and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The source of his wit is clear reason: it is a fountain of that soil; and it springs to vindicate reason, common-sense, rightness and justice; for no vain purpose ever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether comedic ridicule serves to uphold sane moral/intellectual values rather than gratuitously attacking or corrupting; Molière praised for this quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must be stamped in the idea and made permanently human
rubrics_metrics.description: He seized his characters firmly for the central purpose of the play, stamped them in the idea, and by slightly raising and softening the object of study ... generalized upon it so as to make it permanently human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters that exemplify the play’s idea and are sketched so they endure beyond immediate topicality are superior to mere topical caricatures or 'puppets.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal through speech and manner (vivid voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a piece of genius in a writer to make a woman's manner of speech portray her. You feel sensible of her presence in every line of her speaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether dialogue and speech mannerisms reveal character vividly (e.g., Millamant); a living voice is a sign of strong comic characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original study and vigour; avoid stock situations
rubrics_metrics.description: The later imitations ... became tiresome, notwithstanding their fun, in the perpetual recurring of the same situations, owing to the absence of original study and vigour of conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedies should show fresh observation and invention rather than repeat the same recycled situations; penalize dependence on cliché set-pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comedy to teach or expose social absurdities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Femmes Savantes is a capital instance of the uses of comedy in teaching the world to understand what ails it. The farce ... ridiculed and put a stop to the monstrous romantic jargon ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy is praiseworthy when it exposes and corrects social follies by making their absurdity visible (example: Les Femmes Savantes). Score works by civic/diagnostic insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate comic tone: avoid cynical licentiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A cynical licentiousness is more abominable than frank filth. The corrupted importation from France was noxious; a noble entertainment spoiled to suit the wretched taste of a villanous age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone matters: prefer comedy that chastens folly with wit rather than indulging in corrosive cynicism or licentious provocation that lacks redemptive purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle-class cultivated public as ideal audience
rubrics_metrics.description: In all countries the middle class presents the public which, fighting the world, and with a good footing in the fight, knows the world best. Cultivated men and women ... make acute and balanced observers. Molière is their poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a comedy targets and rewards the perceptiveness of a cultivated middle-class audience rather than pandering to the vulgar or the merely sensational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance pathos with humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous writing they will endure, perhaps approve, if it mingles with pathos to shake and elevate the feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that blend humour and pathos to elevate emotional response are stronger than those that provide only shallow amusement; evaluate emotional range alongside wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot should serve an organic idea, not be an afterthought
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot was an afterthought with Congreve. The Way of the World has no idea in it beyond the stale one ... A plot was an afterthought ... By the help of a wooden villain ... he gets a sort of plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plays in which action and plot arise naturally from character and idea rather than contrived devices or late discoveries to force resolution; penalize tacked-on plot conveniences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on epigrams and prepared gags
rubrics_metrics.description: He drives the poor hack word, ‘fool,’ as cruelly to the market for wit ... example (WITWOUD/MIRABEL exchange) is a sort of wit one remembers to have heard at school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of comedy built mainly from slick repartee and prepared jokes; value lines that reveal character or thought rather than only clever quips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language: clarity, simplicity, and purity when appropriate (Molière)
rubrics_metrics.description: He writes purely, in the simplest language, the simplest of French verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate diction for lucidity and appropriateness; simplicity and purity of language can be a virtue when it serves the comic idea, as with Molière, while too ornate phrasing can dilute comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universalize by slight elevation/softening (make topical subjects timeless)
rubrics_metrics.description: By slightly raising and softening the object of study ... generalized upon it so as to make it permanently human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective comedy takes particular social manners and, by modest elevation or softening, makes them speak to universal human traits; score whether a work transcends mere topicality.
